mcqs.question: What makes compare-and-swap (CAS) different from acquiring a lock?
options: CAS can only be used on boolean values
CAS requires the same acquire/release pattern as a lock, just with different syntax
CAS always succeeds on the first attempt, unlike locks which can block
CAS never blocks a thread -- on failure, the thread simply retries with fresh data instead of waiting for anything to be released
mcqs.explanation: The defining difference is that CAS never blocks -- a failed attempt just means retrying immediately with the current value, with nothing 'held' for another thread to wait on. CAS works on integers, references, and more (not just booleans), it doesn't have an acquire/release pattern, and it can absolutely fail and need retries under contention.

mcqs.question: In the lock-free counter's `increment()` loop, why is `compareAndSet(current, next)` called inside a `while` loop instead of just once?
options: Because another thread may have changed the value between the read and the swap attempt, causing the CAS to fail and requiring a retry with fresh data
Because the runtime requires all CAS operations to be attempted exactly three times
Because a single CAS call is not atomic and needs to be repeated to guarantee atomicity
Because the loop is only necessary when more than 100 threads are involved
mcqs.explanation: The loop exists because CAS can fail if the value changed since it was read -- the retry re-reads the current value and tries again. A single CAS call is itself fully atomic; there's no fixed retry count, and the loop is necessary under any level of contention, not just past some thread-count threshold.

mcqs.question: Thread A reads a value as X, pauses, then resumes and sees the value is still X, so its CAS succeeds. Why might this still be unsafe?
options: CAS operations are never actually atomic on real hardware
The value could have been changed away from X and back to X while Thread A was paused (the ABA problem) -- an assumption tied to 'nothing changed' can be silently violated
This scenario is always safe -- if the value matches, nothing relevant could have happened
This can only happen if Thread A is using the wrong data type for the CAS operation
mcqs.explanation: This is exactly the ABA problem: seeing the same value again doesn't prove nothing happened in between, since it could have changed away and back. CAS instructions are genuinely atomic at the hardware level; the danger isn't about data types, and the scenario is specifically NOT always safe -- that's the whole point of the pitfall.

mcqs.question: According to the lock-free vs lock-based comparison, when is lock-free design actually the recommended choice?
options: Whenever multiple fields must be updated together consistently
Whenever code needs to be easier for a new team member to review
For simple state like a single counter or reference, under genuinely high, profiled contention where lock queuing is the proven bottleneck
Always -- lock-free is a strict upgrade over lock-based design in every scenario
mcqs.explanation: The comparison specifically recommends lock-free for simple, single-variable state under proven high contention -- not as a universal default. Multi-field invariants are the case where a lock is usually better, lock-free code is generally harder (not easier) to review, and it is explicitly not a strict upgrade given its added correctness difficulty.
